rows.text: What happens when weight is placed on a bridge?
Traffic, people and the weight of the bridge itself all press on its deck.
To stay standing, the bridge has to carry that load down into the ground.
The load follows a path down through the structure.
The deck is carried by the superstructure, the part of the bridge that spans the gap.
That rests on the substructure: abutments at the ends, and sometimes piers in between.
The abutments pass the load on to the foundations.
Now take a beam bridge.
Its deck rests on long beams that span from one support to the next.
Each beam carries the load by resisting bending.
A cap beam spreads the load onto the posts, and the posts carry it down in compression.
A masonry arch works differently.
It is built from wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs, with a keystone at the crown.
The curve turns the downward load into thrust along the arch, pressing the stones together.

rows.text: So the arch works mainly in compression.

evidence.locator: Part 2 Ratings, Item 25 Arch, p.144 (manual p.2-56)

rows.text: At each end it pushes outward and down on its supports, and the supports push back.

rows.text: The truss we started with takes another approach: straight members joined into triangles.
Each member is mainly pulled or pushed along its length, in tension or in compression.
Each span here is a simple span, so under a downward load its top chord is squeezed and its bottom chord is stretched.
Inside, some web members are in compression and others are in tension.
Let's compare them one at a time.
